Wind energy is one of the leading renewable energy sources, and DFIG-based wind energy conversion systems are widely used due to their variable speed operation and ability to operate in both sub-synchronous and super-synchronous modes.
SSI can lead to equipment damage, power generation loss, and power quality issues in wind-integrated power systems.

The first SSCCI event was reported in 2007 in Minnesota, where a 100 MW DFIG-based wind power plant was accidentally left radially linked to a 345 kV series-compensated transmission line, resulting in oscillations around 9-13 Hz.

In 2009, a similar SSCCI incident occurred in Texas, where a DFIG-based wind power plant connected to a 50-70% fixed series-compensated transmission line experienced oscillations around 22 Hz, causing damage to the series capacitor.
Between 2012 and 2016, the Guyuan wind power system in China experienced more than 58 SSCCI incidents with oscillation frequencies between 6-9 Hz.

Power electronic converters used in wind turbines can generate multiple slip frequencies and negative resistance, which can trigger sub-synchronous oscillations and interact with series-compensated transmission lines or other fast control devices in the power system.
The paper discusses various analysis techniques for SSI, including time-domain simulations, frequency-domain analysis, and modal analysis, each with their own advantages and limitations.

The paper also discusses several mitigation techniques for SSI, such as active damping controllers, converter control modifications, and controlled series compensation, but highlights the challenges and restrictions associated with implementing these techniques in practical power systems.
